1 Maecenas atavis edite regibus,
2 o et praesidium et dulce decus meum:
3 sunt quos curriculo pulverem Olympicum
4 collegisse iuvat metaque fervidis
5 evitata rotis palmaque nobilis
6 terrarum dominos evehit ad deos;
7 hunc, si mobilium turba Quiritium
8 certat tergeminis tollere honoribus,
9 illum, si proprio condidit horreo
10 quidquid de Libycis verritur areis.
11 gaudentem patrios findere sarculo
12 agros Attalicis condicionibus
13 numquam demoveas, ut trabe Cypria
14 Myrtoum pavidus nauta secet mare.
15 luctantem Icariis fluctibus Africum
16 mercator metuens otium et oppidi
17 laudat rura sui; mox reficit rates
18 quassas indocilis pauperiem pati.
19 est qui nec veteris pocula Massici
20 nec partem solido demere de die
21 spernit, nunc viridi membra sub arbuto
22 stratus, nunc ad aquae lene caput sacrae.
23 multos castra iuvant et lituo tubae
24 permixtus sonitus bellaque matribus
25 detestata. manet sub Iove frigido
26 venator tenerae coniugis inmemor,
27 seu visa est catulis cerva fidelibus
28 seu rupit teretes Marsus aper plagas.
29 me doctarum hederae praemia frontium
30 dis miscent superis, me gelidum nemus
31 Nympharumque leves cum Satyris chori
32 secernunt populo, si neque tibias
33 Euterpe cohibet nec Polyhymnia
34 Lesboum refugit tendere barbiton.
35 quodsi me lyricis vatibus inseres,
36 sublimi feriam sidera vertice.

1 Maecenas, born of monarch ancestors, 2 The shield at once and glory of my life! 3 There are who joy them in the Olympic strife 4 And love the dust they gather in the course; 5 The goal by hot wheels shunn'd, the famous prize, 6 Exalt them to the gods that rule mankind; 7 This joys, if rabbles fickle as the wind 8 Through triple grade of honours bid him rise, 9 That, if his granary has stored away 10 Of Libya's thousand floors the yield entire; 11 The man who digs his field as did his sire, 12 With honest pride, no Attalus may sway 13 By proffer'd wealth to tempt Myrtoan seas, 14 The timorous captain of a Cyprian bark. 15 The winds that make Icarian billows dark 16 The merchant fears, and hugs the rural ease 17 Of his own village home; but soon, ashamed 18 Of penury, he refits his batter'd craft. 19 There is, who thinks no scorn of Massic draught, 20 Who robs the daylight of an hour unblamed, 21 Now stretch'd beneath the arbute on the sward, 22 Now by some gentle river's sacred spring; 23 Some love the camp, the clarion's joyous ring, 24 And battle, by the mother's soul abhorr'd. 25 See, patient waiting in the clear keen air, 26 The hunter, thoughtless of his delicate bride, 27 Whether the trusty hounds a stag have eyed, 28 Or the fierce Marsian boar has burst the snare. 29 To me the artist's meed, the ivy wreath 30 Is very heaven: me the sweet cool of woods, 31 Where Satyrs frolic with the Nymphs, secludes 32 From rabble rout, so but Euterpe's breath 33 Fail not the flute, nor Polyhymnia fly 34 Averse from stringing new the Lesbian lyre. 35 O, write my name among that minstrel choir, 36 And my proud head shall strike upon the sky!

1 Iam satis terris nivis atque dirae
2 grandinis misit pater et rubente
3 dextera sacras iaculatus arcis
4 terruit urbem,
5 terruit gentis, grave ne rediret
6 saeculum Pyrrhae nova monstra questae,
7 omne cum Proteus pecus egit altos
8 visere montis,
9 piscium et summa genus haesit ulmo,
10 nota quae sedes fuerat columbis,
11 et superiecto pavidae natarunt
12 aequore dammae.
13 vidimus flavum Tiberim retortis
14 litore Etrusco violenter undis
15 ire deiectum monumenta regis
16 templaque Vestae,
17 Iliae dum se nimium querenti
18 iactat ultorem, vagus et sinistra

22 quo graves Persae melius perirent,

24 rara iuventus.

1 Enough of snow and hail at last 2 The sire has sent in vengeance down: 3 His bolts, at his own temple cast, 4 Appall'd the town, 5 Appall'd the lands, lest Pyrrha's time 6 Return, with all its monstrous sights, 7 When Proteus led his flocks to climb 8 The flatten'd heights, 9 When fish were in the elm-tops caught, 10 Where once the stock-dove wont to bide, 11 And does were floating, all distraught, 12 Adown the tide. 13 Old Tiber, hurl'd in tumult back 14 From mingling with the Etruscan main, 15 Has threaten'd Numa's court with wrack 16 And Vesta's fane. 17 Roused by his Ilia's plaintive woes, 18 He vows revenge for guiltless blood, 19 And, spite of Jove, his banks o'erflows, 20 Uxorious flood. 21 Yes, Fame shall tell of civic steel 22 That better Persian lives had spilt, 23 To youths, whose minish'd numbers feel 24 Their parents' guilt. 25 What god shall Rome invoke to stay 26 Her fall? Can suppliance overbear 27 The ear of Vesta, turn'd away 28 From chant and prayer? 29 Who comes, commission'd to atone 30 For crime like ours? at length appear,

31 nube candentis umeros amictus
32 augur Apollo;
33 sive tu mavis, Erycina ridens,
34 quam Iocus circum volat et Cupido;
35 sive neglectum genus et nepotes
36 respicis, auctor
37 heu nimis longo satiate ludo,
38 quem iuvat clamor galeaeque leves
39 acer et Marsi peditis cruentum
40 voltus in hostem;
41 sive mutata iuvenem figura
42 ales in terris imitaris almae
43 filius Maiae, patiens vocari
44 Caesaris ultor:
45 serus in caelum redeas diuque
46 laetus intersis populo Quirini
47 neve te nostris vitiis iniquum
48 ocior aura
49 tollat; hic magnos potius triumphos,
50 hic ames dici pater atque princeps
51 neu sinas Medos equitare inultos
52 te duce, Caesar.

31 A cloud round thy bright shoulders thrown, 32 Apollo seer! 33 Or Venus, laughter-loving dame, 34 Round whom gay Loves and Pleasures fly; 35 Or thou, if slighted sons may claim 36 A parent's eye, 37 O weary with thy long, long game, 38 Who lov'st fierce shouts and helmets bright, 39 And Moorish warrior's glance of flame 40 Or e'er he smite! 41 Or Maia's son, if now awhile 42 In youthful guise we see thee here, 43 Caesar's avenger—such the style 44 Thou deign'st to bear; 45 Late be thy journey home, and long 46 Thy sojourn with Rome's family; 47 Nor let thy wrath at our great wrong 48 Lend wings to fly. 49 Here take our homage, Chief and Sire; 50 Here wreathe with bay thy conquering brow, 51 And bid the prancing Mede retire, 52 Our Caesar thou!

1 Sic te diva potens Cypri,
2 sic fratres Helenae, lucida sidera,
3 ventorumque regat pater
4 obstrictis aliis praeter Iapyga,
5 navis, quae tibi creditum
6 debes Vergilium; finibus Atticis
7 reddas incolumem precor
8 et serves animae dimidium meae.
9 illi robur et aes triplex
10 circa pectus erat, qui fragilem truci
11 conmisit pelago ratem
12 primus: nec timuit praecipitem Africum
13 decertantem Aquilonibus
14 nec tristis Hyadas nec rabiem Noti,
15 quo non arbiter Hadriae
16 maior, tollere seu ponere volt freta;
17 quem mortis timuit gradum
18 qui siccis oculis monstra natantia,
19 qui vidit mare turbidum et
20 infamis scopulos Acroceraunia?
21 nequiquam deus abscidit
22 prudens oceano dissociabili
23 terras, si tamen inpiae
24 non tangenda rates transiliunt vada.
25 audax omnia perpeti
26 gens humana ruit per vetitum nefas:
27 audax Iapeti genus
28 ignem fraude mala gentibus intulit;
29 post ignem aetheria domo
30 subductum macies et nova febrium
31 terris incubuit cohors
32 semotique prius tarda necessitas
33 Leti corripuit gradum;
34 expertus vacuum Daedalus aera
35 pennis non homini datis;
36 perrupit Acheronta Herculeus labor.
37 nil mortalibus ardui est:
38 caelum ipsum petimus stultitia neque
39 per nostrum patimur scelus
40 iracunda Iovem ponere fulmina.

1 Thus may Cyprus' heavenly queen, 2 Thus Helen's brethren, stars of brightest sheen, 3 Guide thee! May the sire of wind 4 Each truant gale, save only Zephyr, bind! 5 So do thou, fair ship, that ow'st 6 Virgil, thy precious freight, to Attic coast, 7 Safe restore thy loan and whole, 8 And save from death the partner of my soul! 9 Oak and brass of triple fold 10 Encompass'd sure that heart, which first made bold 11 To the raging sea to trust 12 A fragile bark, nor fear'd the Afric gust 13 With its Northern mates at strife, 14 Nor Hyads' frown, nor South-wind fury-rife, 15 Mightiest power that Hadria knows, 16 Wills he the waves to madden or compose. 17 What had Death in store to awe 18 Those eyes, that huge sea-beasts unmelting saw, 19 Saw the swelling of the surge, 20 And high Ceraunian cliffs, the seaman's scourge? 21 Heaven's high providence in vain 22 Has sever'd countries with the estranging main, 23 If our vessels ne'ertheless 24 With reckless plunge that sacred bar transgress. 25 Daring all, their goal to win, 26 Men tread forbidden ground, and rush on sin: 27 Daring all, Prometheus play'd 28 His wily game, and fire to man convey'd; 29 Soon as fire was stolen away, 30 Pale Fever's stranger host and wan Decay 31 Swept o'er earth's polluted face, 32 And slow Fate quicken'd Death's once halting pace. 33 Daedalus the void air tried 34 On wings, to humankind by Heaven denied; 35 Acheron's bar gave way with ease 36 Before the arm of labouring Hercules. 37 Nought is there for man too high; 38 Our impious folly e'en would climb the sky, 39 Braves the dweller on the steep, 40 Nor lets the bolts of heavenly vengeance sleep.

1 Solvitur acris hiems grata vice veris et Favoni
2 trahuntque siccas machinae carinas
3 ac neque iam stabulis gaudet pecus aut arator igni
4 nec prata canis albicant pruinis.
5 iam Cytherea choros ducit Venus imminente luna
6 iunctaeque Nymphis Gratiae decentes
7 alterno terram quatiunt pede, dum gravis Cyclopum
8 Volcanus ardens visit officinas.
9 nunc decet aut viridi nitidum caput impedire myrto
10 aut flore, terrae quem ferunt solutae,
11 nunc et in umbrosis Fauno decet immolare lucis,
12 seu poscat agna sive malit haedo.
13 pallida Mors aequo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas
14 regumque turris. o beate Sesti,
15 vitae summa brevis spem nos vetat inchoare longam;
16 iam te premet nox fabulaeque Manes
17 et domus exilis Plutonia; quo simul mearis,
18 nec regna vini sortiere talis
19 nec tenerum Lycidan mirabere, quo calet iuventus
20 nunc omnis et mox virgines tepebunt.

1 The touch of Zephyr and of Spring has loosen'd Winter's thrall; 2 The well-dried keels are wheel'd again to sea: 3 The ploughman cares not for his fire, nor cattle for their stall, 4 And frost no more is whitening all the lea. 5 Now Cytherea leads the dance, the bright moon overhead; 6 The Graces and the Nymphs, together knit, 7 With rhythmic feet the meadow beat, while Vulcan, fiery red, 8 Heats the Cyclopian forge in Aetna's pit. 9 'Tis now the time to wreathe the brow with branch of myrtle green, 10 Or flowers, just opening to the vernal breeze; 11 Now Faunus claims his sacrifice among the shady treen, 12 Lambkin or kidling, which soe'er he please. 13 Pale Death, impartial, walks his round: he knocks at cottage-gate 14 And palace-portal. Sestius, child of bliss! 15 How should a mortal's hopes be long, when short his being's date? 16 Lo here! the fabulous ghosts, the dark abyss, 17 The void of the Plutonian hall, where soon as e'er you go, 18 No more for you shall leap the auspicious die 19 To seat you on the throne of wine; no more your breast shall glow 20 For Lycidas, the star of every eye.

1 Quis multa gracilis te puer in rosa
2 perfusus liquidis urget odoribus
3 grato, Pyrrha, sub antro?
4 cui flavam religas comam
5 simplex munditiis? heu quotiens fidem
6 mutatosque deos flebit et aspera
7 nigris aequora ventis
8 emirabitur insolens
9 qui nunc te fruitur credulus aurea,
10 qui semper vacuam, semper amabilem
11 sperat, nescius aurae
12 fallacis. miseri, quibus
13 intemptata nites. me tabula sacer
14 votiva paries indicat uvida
15 suspendisse potenti
16 vestimenta maris deo.

1 What slender youth, besprinkled with perfume, 2 Courts you on roses in some grotto's shade? 3 Fair Pyrrha, say, for whom 4 Your yellow hair you braid, 5 So trim, so simple! Ah! how oft shall he 6 Lament that faith can fail, that gods can change, 7 Viewing the rough black sea 8 With eyes to tempests strange, 9 Who now is basking in your golden smile, 10 And dreams of you still fancy-free, still kind, 11 Poor fool, nor knows the guile 12 Of the deceitful wind! 13 Woe to the eyes you dazzle without cloud 14 Untried! For me, they show in yonder fane 15 My dripping garments, vow'd 16 To Him who curbs the main.

1 Scriberis Vario fortis et hostium
2 victor Maeonii carminis alite,
3 quam rem cumque ferox navibus aut equis
4 miles te duce gesserit.
5 nos, Agrippa, neque haec dicere nec gravem
6 Pelidae stomachum cedere nescii
7 nec cursus duplicis per mare Ulixei
8 nec saevam Pelopis domum
9 conamur, tenues grandia, dum pudor
10 inbellisque lyrae Musa potens vetat
11 laudes egregii Caesaris et tuas
12 culpa deterere ingeni.
13 quis Martem tunica tectum adamantina
14 digne scripserit aut pulvere Troico
15 nigrum Merionen aut ope Palladis
16 Tydiden superis parem?
17 nos convivia, nos proelia virginum
18 sectis in iuvenes unguibus acrium
19 cantamus, vacui sive quid urimur,
20 non praeter solitum leves.

1 Not I, but Varius:—he, of Homer's brood 2 A tuneful swan, shall bear you on his wing, 3 Your tale of trophies, won by field or flood, 4 Mighty alike to sing. 5 Not mine such themes, Agrippa; no, nor mine 6 To chant the Wrath that fill'd Pelides' breast, 7 Nor dark Ulysses' wanderings o'er the brine, 8 Nor Pelops' house unblest. 9 Vast were the task, I feeble; inborn shame, 10 And she, who makes the peaceful lyre submit, 11 Forbid me to impair great Caesar's fame 12 And yours by my weak wit. 13 But who may fitly sing of Mars array'd 14 In adamant mail, or Merion, black with dust 15 Of Troy, or Tydeus' son by Pallas' aid 16 Strong against gods to thrust? 17 Feasts are my theme, my warriors maidens fair, 18 Who with pared nails encounter youths in fight; 19 Be Fancy free or caught in Cupid's snare, 20 Her temper still is light.

1 Laudabunt alii claram Rhodon aut Mytilenen
2 aut Epheson bimarisve Corinthi
3 moenia vel Baccho Thebas vel Apolline Delphos
4 insignis aut Thessala Tempe;
5 sunt quibus unum opus est intactae Palladis urbem
6 carmine perpetuo celebrare et
7 undique decerptam fronti praeponere olivam;
8 plurimus in Iunonis honorem
9 aptum dicet equis Argos ditisque Mycenas:
10 me nec tam patiens Lacedaemon
11 nec tam Larisae percussit campus opimae
12 quam domus Albuneae resonantis
13 et praeceps Anio ac Tiburni lucus et uda
14 mobilibus pomaria rivis.
15 albus ut obscuro deterget nubila caelo
16 saepe Notus neque parturit imbris
17 perpetuos, sic tu sapiens finire memento
18 tristitiam vitaeque labores
19 molli, Plance, mero, seu te fulgentia signis
20 castra tenent seu densa tenebit
21 Tiburis umbra tui. Teucer Salamina patremque
22 cum fugeret, tamen uda Lyaeo
23 tempora populea fertur vinxisse corona
24 sic tristis adfatus amicos:
25 “quo nos cumque feret melior fortuna parente,
26 ibimus—o socii comitesque,
27 nil desperandum Teucro duce et auspice Teucro:
28 certus enim promisit Apollo
29 ambiguam tellure nova Salamina futuram.
30 o fortes peioraque passi
31 mecum saepe viri, nunc vino pellite curas;
32 cras ingens iterabimus aequor.”

1 Let others Rhodes or Mytilene sing, 2 Or Ephesus, or Corinth, set between 3 Two seas, or Thebes, or Delphi, for its king 4 Each famous, or Thessalian Tempe green; 5 There are who make chaste Pallas' virgin tower 6 The daily burden of unending song, 7 And search for wreaths the olive's rifled bower: 8 The praise of Juno sounds from many a tongue, 9 Telling of Argos' steeds, Mycenae's gold. 10 For me stern Sparta forges no such spell, 11 No, nor Larissa's plain of richest mould, 12 As bright Albunea echoing from her cell. 13 O headlong Anio! O Tiburnian groves, 14 And orchards saturate with shifting streams! 15 Look how the clear fresh south from heaven removes 16 The tempest, nor with rain perpetual teems! 17 You too be wise, my Plancus: life's worst cloud 18 Will melt in air, by mellow wine allay'd, 19 Dwell you in camps, with glittering banners proud, 20 Or 'neath your Tibur's canopy of shade. 21 When Teucer fled before his father's frown 22 From Salamis, they say his temples deep 23 He dipp'd in wine, then wreath'd with poplar crown, 24 And bade his comrades lay their grief to sleep: 25 “Where Fortune bears us, than my sire more kind, 26 There let us go, my own, my gallant crew. 27 'Tis Teucer leads, 'tis Teucer breathes the wind; 28 No more despair; Apollo's word is true. 29 Another Salamis in kindlier air 30 Shall yet arise. Hearts, that have borne with me 31 Worse buffets! drown today in wine your care; 32 To-morrow we recross the wide, wide sea!”

1 Lydia, dic per omnis
2 te deos oro, Sybarin cur properes amando
3 perdere, cur apricum
4 oderit campum patiens pulveris atque solis,
5 cur neque militaris
6 inter aequalis equitet, Gallica nec lupatis
7 temperet ora frenis?
8 cur timet flavum Tiberim tangere? cur olivum
9 sanguine viperino
10 cautius vitat neque iam livida gestat armis
11 bracchia saepe disco,
12 saepe trans finem iaculo nobilis expedito?
13 quid latet, ut marinae
14 filium dicunt Thetidis sub lacrimosa Troiae
15 funera, ne virilis
16 cultus in caedem et Lycias proriperet catervas?

1 Lydia, by all above, 2 Why bear so hard on Sybaris, to ruin him with love? 3 What change has made him shun 4 The playing-ground, who once so well could bear the dust and sun? 5 Why does he never sit 6 On horseback in his company, nor with uneven bit 7 His Gallic courser tame? 8 Why dreads he yellow Tiber, as 'twould sully that fair frame? 9 Like poison loathes the oil, 10 His arms no longer black and blue with honourable toil, 11 He who erewhile was known 12 For quoit or javelin oft and oft beyond the limit thrown? 13 Why skulks he, as they say 14 Did Thetis' son before the dawn of Ilion's fatal day, 15 For fear the manly dress 16 Should fling him into danger's arms, amid the 17 Lycian press?

1 Vides ut alta stet nive candidum
2 Soracte nec iam sustineant onus
3 silvae laborantes geluque
4 flumina constiterint acuto?
5 dissolve frigus ligna super foco
6 large reponens atque benignius
7 deprome quadrimum Sabina,
8 o Thaliarche, merum diota.
9 permitte divis cetera, qui simul
10 stravere ventos aequore fervido
11 deproeliantis, nec cupressi
12 nec veteres agitantur orni.
13 quid sit futurum cras, fuge quaerere et
14 quem Fors dierum cumque dabit, lucro
15 adpone nec dulcis amores
16 sperne puer neque tu choreas,
17 donec virenti canities abest
18 morosa. nunc et campus et areae
19 lenesque sub noctem susurri
20 conposita repetantur hora,
21 nunc et latentis proditor intumo
22 gratus puellae risus ab angulo
23 pignusque dereptum lacertis
24 aut digito male pertinaci.

1 See, how it stands, one pile of snow, 2 Soracte! 'neath the pressure yield 3 Its groaning woods; the torrents' flow 4 With clear sharp ice is all congeal'd. 5 Heap high the logs, and melt the cold, 6 Good Thaliarch; draw the wine we ask, 7 That mellower vintage, four-year-old, 8 From out the cellar'd Sabine cask. 9 The future trust with Jove; when he 10 Has still'd the warring tempests' roar 11 On the vex'd deep, the cypress-tree 12 And aged ash are rock'd no more. 13 O, ask not what the morn will bring, 14 But count as gain each day that chance 15 May give you; sport in life's young spring, 16 Nor scorn sweet love, nor merry dance, 17 While years are green, while sullen eld 18 Is distant. Now the walk, the game, 19 The whisper'd talk at sunset held, 20 Each in its hour, prefer their claim. 21 Sweet too the laugh, whose feign'd alarm 22 The hiding-place of beauty tells, 23 The token, ravish'd from the arm 24 Or finger, that but ill rebels.

1 Mercuri facunde nepos Atlantis,
2 qui feros cultus hominum recentum
3 voce formasti catus et decorae
4 more palaestrae,
5 te canam, magni Iovis et deorum
6 nuntium curvaeque lyrae parentem,
7 callidum, quidquid placuit, iocoso
8 condere furto.
9 te, boves olim nisi reddidisses
10 per dolum amotas, puerum minaci
11 voce dum terret, viduus pharetra
12 risit Apollo.
13 quin et Atridas duce te superbos
14 Ilio dives Priamus relicto
15 Thessalosque ignis et iniqua Troiae
16 castra fefellit.
17 tu pias laetis animas reponis
18 sedibus virgaque levem coerces
19 aurea turbam, superis deorum
20 gratus et imis.

1 Grandson of Atlas, wise of tongue, 2 O Mercury, whose wit could tame 3 Man's savage youth by power of song 4 And plastic game! 5 Thee sing I, herald of the sky, 6 Who gav'st the lyre its music sweet, 7 Hiding whate'er might please thine eye 8 In frolic cheat. 9 See, threatening thee, poor guileless child, 10 Apollo claims, in angry tone, 11 His cattle;—all at once he smiled, 12 His quiver gone. 13 Strong in thy guidance, Hector's sire 14 Escaped the Atridae, pass'd between 15 Thessalian tents and warders' fire, 16 Of all unseen, 17 Thou lay'st unspotted souls to rest; 18 Thy golden rod pale spectres know; 19 Blest power! by all thy brethren blest, 20 Above, below!

1 Tu ne quaesieris, scire nefas, quem mihi, quem tibi
2 finem di dederint, Leuconoe, nec Babylonios
3 temptaris numeros. ut melius, quidquid erit, pati.
4 seu pluris hiemes seu tribuit Iuppiter ultimam,
5 quae nunc oppositis debilitat pumicibus mare
6 Tyrrhenum: sapias, vina liques et spatio brevi
7 spem longam reseces. dum loquimur, fugerit invida
8 aetas: carpe diem quam minimum credula postero.

1 Ask not ('tis forbidden knowledge), what our destined term of years, 2 Mine and yours; nor scan the tables of your Babylonish seers. 3 Better far to bear the future, my Leuconoe, like the past, 4 Whether Jove has many winters yet to give, or this our last; 5 This, that makes the Tyrrhene billows spend their strength against the shore. 6 Strain your wine and prove your wisdom; life is short; should hope be more? 7 In the moment of our talking, envious time has ebb'd away. 8 Seize the present; trust tomorrow e'en as little as you may.

1 Quem virum aut heroa lyra vel acri
2 tibia sumis celebrare, Clio?
3 quem deum? cuius recinet iocosa
4 nomen imago
5 aut in umbrosis Heliconis oris
6 aut super Pindo gelidove in Haemo?
7 unde vocalem temere insecutae
8 Orphea silvae,
9 arte materna rapidos morantem
10 fluminum lapsus celeresque ventos,
11 blandum et auritas fidibus canoris
12 ducere quercus.
13 quid prius dicam solitis parentis
14 laudibus, qui res hominum ac deorum,
15 qui mare ac terras variisque mundum
16 temperat horis?
17 unde nil maius generatur ipso
18 nec viget quidquam simile aut secundum.
19 proximos illi tamen occupavit
20 Pallas honores
21 proeliis audax. neque te silebo,
22 Liber et saevis inimica virgo
23 beluis, nec te, metuende certa
24 Phoebe sagitta.
25 dicam et Alciden puerosque Ledae,
26 hunc equis, illum superare pugnis
27 nobilem; quorum simul alba nautis
28 stella refulsit,
29 defluit saxis agitatus umor,
30 concidunt venti fugiuntque nubes

1 What man, what hero, Clio sweet, 2 On harp or flute wilt thou proclaim? 3 What god shall echo's voice repeat 4 In mocking game 5 To Helicon's sequester'd shade, 6 Or Pindus, or on Haemus chill, 7 Where once the hurrying woods obey'd 8 The minstrel's will, 9 Who, by his mother's gift of song, 10 Held the fleet stream, the rapid breeze, 11 And led with blandishment along 12 The listening trees? 13 Whom praise we first? the sire on high, 14 Who gods and men unerring guides, 15 Who rules the sea, the earth, the sky, 16 Their times and tides. 17 No mightier birth may he beget; 18 No like, no second has he known; 19 Yet nearest to her sire's is set 20 Minerva's throne. 21 Nor yet shall Bacchus pass unsaid, 22 Bold warrior, nor the virgin foe 23 Of savage beasts, nor Phoebus, dread 24 With deadly bow. 25 Alcides too shall be my theme, 26 And Leda's twins, for horses he, 27 He famed for boxing; soon as gleam 28 Their stars at sea, 29 The lash'd spray trickles from the steep, 30 The wind sinks down, the storm-cloud flies,

31 et minax, quia sic voluere, ponto
32 unda recumbit.
